scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Welcome back! Last time we ran one program. Today we set up your computer so you can run your own. It takes about ten minutes, and you only do it once.

scenes.onScreen: "What you need": three numbered lines and a kitchen analogy card
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the kitchen card slides in with a chopping board, a stove and a chef
scenes.narration: You need three things. Python itself. An editor, where you type, like VS Code. And a terminal, where you give commands. Think of a kitchen. Python is the stove, the editor is the chopping board, and the terminal is you, giving the orders. Do not worry if the names sound strange. By the end of today, you have typed every one of these commands yourself.

lines: An editor, where you type, like VS Code.
And a terminal, where you give commands.

scenes.onScreen: Install steps for Windows, Mac and Linux, shown as three tabs
scenes.animation: Three tabs (Windows, Mac, Linux) switch with a pop; the active steps tick in one by one
scenes.narration: Go to python dot org, open Downloads, and install the latest version. On Windows, tick the box that says, add Python to PATH. On a Mac, run the installer. On Linux, Python is usually already there. Then open a terminal and type python, space, dash dash version. If a number appears, you are ready. On some Macs and Linux machines, the command is python three.

lines: On a Mac, run the installer.
On Linux, Python is usually already there.
If a number appears, you are ready.

scenes.onScreen: Two boxes: the REPL, one line and an answer at once; a script, many lines in a saved .py file
scenes.animation: Two boxes pop in side by side; in the left box a line types and its answer appears at once; in the right box a saved file runs top to bottom
scenes.narration: Python has two ways to run code. In the REPL, you type one line and get the answer at once. It is great for tiny tests. In a script, you save many lines in a file that ends in dot py, and run the whole file. We mostly use scripts. You can keep them, fix them, and run them again.

lines: Python has two ways to run code.
It is great for tiny tests.

scenes.onScreen: fish.py: two names, a label and a total
scenes.animation: Same code; the output panel fills line by line with a ding per output line; [TRACK] cards update
scenes.narration: [HL 1] [TRACK fish=3] Make a name called fish, and put three in it. [HL 2] [TRACK price=120] A name called price, one hundred twenty. [HL 3] Print a label, then the value. Print puts a space between the things for you. [HL 4] And Python does the maths: fish times price. Three times one hundred twenty is three hundred sixty.

code.source:
fish = 3
price = 120
print("Fish:", fish)
print("Total:", fish * price)

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as fish dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, fish dot py. Fish, three. Total, three hundred sixty. Always check that you are in the same folder as the file.

scenes.onScreen: Recap: four steps on one card
scenes.animation: Four recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Recap time. One: you need Python, an editor and a terminal. Two: check Python with python, dash dash version. Three: save your code in a file that ends in dot py. Four: run it with python, a space, and the file name. If any step fails, do not panic. Read the message, check the spelling, and try again. Every programmer does this, every single day.

lines: You need Python, an editor and a terminal.
Check Python with python, dash dash version.
Save your code in a file that ends in dot py.
Run it with python, a space, and the file name.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: print with a capital P
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We wrote print with a capital P. Python says, name error, Print is not defined. And it even asks, did you mean print, with a small p? Python is case sensitive. Capital P and small p are different names. Fix the letter, and it works.

props.error:
File "fish.py", line 2, in <module>
    Print("Fish:", fish)
    ^^^^^
NameError: name 'Print' is not defined. Did you mean: 'print'?

lines: NameError: name 'Print' is not defined. Did you mean: 'print'?

props.why: Python treats upper and lower case as different letters, so Print and print are two different names.

shorts.title: What you need for Python
shorts.script: Three tools, ten minutes. To write Python you need Python itself, an editor like VS Code, and a terminal. Think of a kitchen. Python is the stove, the editor is the chopping board, and the terminal is you, giving the orders. You only set this up once. After that, you can run your own programs whenever you like. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Set up Python in three steps.

shorts.title: Check your install
shorts.script: Is Python really installed? Open a terminal and type python, space, dash dash version. If a number appears, you are ready to go. On some Macs and Linux machines, the command is python three instead. On Windows, remember to tick the box that says, add Python to PATH, when you install. One quick command tells you everything. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: One command to check.

shorts.title: REPL versus script
shorts.script: Two ways to run Python. The REPL runs one line at a time, and shows the answer at once, which is great for tiny tests. A script is a saved file that ends in dot py, and it runs from top to bottom. Use the REPL to experiment, and use scripts for real programs you want to keep. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: REPL or script?

shorts.title: Print is not defined
shorts.script: One capital letter breaks everything. Write Print with a capital P, and Python says, name error, Print is not defined. It even asks, did you mean print with a small p? Python is case sensitive, so capital and small letters are different names. The fix is just one letter. Read the hint at the bottom of the error. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python is case sensitive.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.script: A snake lost in a folder. Why? It kept running the wrong dot py. Now your challenge. Install Python, and check the version. Then run fish dot py from the same folder, and read the output. Change the price to one hundred fifty, and run it again. What total do you get? Tell us in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 02.
shorts.caption: Do the challenge.
